# iOS Home-Screen Widget is a WidgetKit extension generated by @bacons/apple-targets

ADR 0017 shipped the **Home-Screen Widget** on Android. The iOS half reuses both of its load-bearing decisions unchanged — hand-written native rendering, and unauthenticated fetches against the public `GET /users/:handle/profile` endpoint with only the handle, theme preference and API origin shared out of the app. What iOS adds is a target-generation problem Android didn't have.

An Android AppWidget is a receiver in the app's own process, so it rode along in the local Expo module's library manifest and prebuild's manifest merge picked it up. A WidgetKit widget is a separate Xcode target with its own bundle, deployment target, entitlements and product type — and `ios/` is prebuild output that is never checked in, so the target has to be regenerated from source on every prebuild. We use **`@bacons/apple-targets`**: `targets/widget/` holds the Swift and the target config, and the plugin links it into the generated project. Hand-rolling the same pbxproj surgery in a bespoke config plugin was rejected — it is a few hundred lines of Xcode-project manipulation to maintain against Xcode releases, in exchange for one widget target.

The app and the extension are different processes, so the shared state moves through an **app group** (`group.com.rowanpaul.opnshelf`) instead of Android's `SharedPreferences`. It is declared once under `ios.entitlements` in `app.config.ts` and mirrored onto the widget target by `targets/widget/expo-target.config.js`. The suite name and its four keys are duplicated between `modules/widget-bridge/ios/WidgetBridgeModule.swift` and `targets/widget/index.swift`: Apple extensions are separate compilation units, and a shared framework for four string constants costs more than the duplication.

Freshness is a WidgetKit timeline with one hourly entry, pre-empted by `WidgetCenter.reloadAllTimelines()` on watch log/remove, login, logout, and theme change — the same trigger set as Android, through the same JS bridge. Hourly is the practical floor: iOS budgets widget refreshes and treats the policy as a hint, so the app-triggered reloads carry most of the freshness and the timeline is the backstop for watches logged elsewhere.

Consequences: adding an Apple target means `ios/` must be regenerated (`npx expo prebuild -p ios --clean`) after pulling this change, and the widget's app-group entitlement makes the app's provisioning profile capability-bearing — EAS has to reissue it on the first build. As on Android, the widget cannot ship via EAS Update, and it shows the signed-in user's own graph only. Widget families are limited to `systemSmall` and `systemMedium`; a 30-bar graph has nothing useful to do with `systemLarge`'s height. Deployment target is iOS 17 (`containerBackground(for:)`), above the app's own minimum — older devices simply see no widget offered.
